name: Democratic republic
summary: A democratic republic is a state without a hereditary head in which the people hold ultimate political power and choose their leaders by election, under a constitution and law. Tocqueville's account of the American case adds that it is kept alive by federal form, local self-government, independent courts and free press, and that it is endangered by the tyranny of the majority. It prescribes a form of rule, not an economic or cultural programme.

scope: The form of government the name describes: a republic (no monarch, rulers chosen by the people's election) run on democratic principles, as EBSCO's research starter on the republic defines it and as Tocqueville analyses it in Democracy in America (volume 1, with volume 2 naming the type). It excludes states that only carry the name (the German Democratic Republic, Democratic People's Republic of Korea), the Marxist-Leninist people's democracies, and the neighbouring subjects of republicanism, representative democracy and liberal democracy.

Tocqueville describes the American case and often weighs pros and cons rather than prescribing, so his answers are medium at most; he does not settle economy, society, culture, ecology, technology or world statements. Britannica, Merriam-Webster and ScienceDirect refused access (403) and were not worked around. Suffrage limits are left open by EBSCO (universal suffrage is not required), so franchise statements are null.
